read: full: all 19 pages (abstract, sections 1-10, references, Appendix A task catalogue, Appendix B run artifacts).
venue_now: arXiv preprint 2606.20950v2 [cs.AI], 2 July 2026 (p.1 margin stamp); single author; no venue shown.
what_it_is: An executable benchmark for power-engineering agents: 41 task families in eight areas (network analysis, short circuit and protection, stability and grid code, distributed resources, microgrids and dispatch, reliability and restoration, power quality and standards, forecasting), each grounded in a cited standard, textbook method or paper (p.1, p.7-8). An agent reads a structured task and writes a structured JSON solution; a deterministic evaluator recomputes the engineering quantities, checks hard constraints, and returns a feasibility flag, a score normalised to the reference optimum and a list of violations, and the agent's rationale is excluded from scoring (p.2, p.5, p.8). The public split has one case per family; held-out cases are produced on demand by per-family generators that redraw a public case's numbers under a private seed and keep a draw only if the reference solver solves it (p.6-7). Three command-line agents score near the ceiling on both splits (p.10).
domain: engineering: electrical power systems (8 areas, 41 task families)
size: 41 task families, one public case each (41 public cases); held-out cases generated on demand, 41 per reference round and 328 in the generator validation (p.10-11). Reference round: three agent configurations (Codex/gpt-5.5, Cursor/composer-2.5, OpenCode/deepseek-v4-flash-free); public-split grid: four further models under two harnesses (p.9, p.11-12).
source_of_items: author-built executable cases, each grounded in a cited standard, textbook method or documented formulation, with a declared confidence: 11 high, 28 medium, 2 low (p.8, Appendix A p.17-19). Held-out cases are perturbed from the public case by per-family generators (p.6-7).
instances: generated: one static public case per family, plus held-out cases synthesised on demand from a private seed by deterministic, physics-aware perturbation of the public case (p.6-7)
has_gold_traces: no: each family has a reference solver that computes the answer or optimum (p.8), but no intermediate reasoning is supplied or checked; the agent's rationale is recorded only for diagnosis (p.2-3).
evaluation: unit tests (executable, deterministic): the evaluator recomputes quantities from the submitted structured solution; exact computations pass within a 0.1% relative band with a small absolute floor, optimisation tasks score the gap to the reference optimum, classification tasks are scored against exact sets, and compliance tasks are pass/fail (p.8-9). Run-level feasible rate, perfect rate and mean score (p.9). The evaluators are compact surrogates (closed-form methods or simplified models such as a linear voltage-sensitivity stand-in for AC power flow), not full simulators (p.5-6, p.12). Outcome-level only: no step-level scoring.
human_validation: Limited. 'Each task was checked for physical correctness against its cited source before inclusion' (p.7), with no count or agreement figure. Three evaluators are cross-checked against golden cases derived by hand from the governing formulas (p.9). The main quality control is reading unanimous agent failures as likely specification or evaluator defects; this found an off-by-one error in the faulted-section evaluator that the self-consistency check had missed, because the reference solver was derived from the same function as the evaluator (p.10-11). No expert labels of agent outputs.
contamination_measures: private test set: held-out cases are synthesised on demand from a private seed by inspectable per-family generators, and only aggregate held-out results are published (p.6-7, p.19). Public and held-out scores are broadly consistent (held-out marginally higher) (p.10); the paper calls the protection 'prospective' (p.13).

engtrace_use.explanation: Candidate; the May paper does not cite it, and it does not cite EngTrace. It is the engineering precedent for two of EngTrace's design choices: deterministic recomputation of engineering quantities against a tolerance (p.8-9), and held-out instances generated from a private seed so that construction is auditable while instances stay private (p.6-7).

suggested_wording: The Power Systems Agent Benchmark (Trashchenkov, 2026) checks agents' structured solutions to 41 power-engineering task families with deterministic evaluators that recompute the engineering quantities, and generates its held-out cases from a private seed to limit contamination; it scores the submitted solution, not the reasoning behind it.
facts_to_cite: 41 task families across eight areas of electric power engineering, each grounded in a cited standard, textbook method or documented formulation (p.1, p.7-8)

A deterministic evaluator recomputes the engineering quantities, checks hard constraints and returns a feasibility flag, a score normalised to the reference optimum and a list of violations; the agent's natural-language rationale is excluded from scoring (p.2, p.5, p.8)
Exact computations are scored within a 0.1% relative tolerance with a small absolute floor (p.8-9)
Held-out cases are synthesised on demand by per-family generators from a private seed, accepted only if the reference solver solves them; only aggregate held-out results are published (p.6-7)
Generator validation: 328 held-out variants (41 x 8), all feasible, with 40 of 41 families giving eight distinct instances (p.11)
Three command-line agents score 0.951 to 0.973 on the public split and 0.973 to 1.000 on the held-out split (Table 1, p.10)
The evaluators are compact deterministic surrogates, not full power-system simulators (p.5-6, p.12)
Unanimous agent failures exposed an evaluator bug that self-consistency checks missed, because the reference solver and the evaluator shared the same function (p.10-11)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: an engineering domain (electrical power, next to but not overlapping EngTrace's electrical domains of communications, electromagnetics and signals); generated instances from a private seed with an inspectable construction, which is EngTrace's contamination design (p.6-7); deterministic checking of computed engineering quantities against a tight numeric tolerance (p.8-9); grounding of each task in standards and textbooks (p.8). Lacks: gold reasoning traces and any step-level evaluation (the rationale is excluded from scoring, p.2); multi-branch scope (one branch); expert validation of the evaluator (three hand-derived golden cases and agent-agreement QC only, p.9-11); difficulty tiers; a sizeable public set (one case per family, which the paper calls statistically fragile, p.12). It evaluates agents' structured outputs, not free-text reasoning. What EngTrace adds beyond it: gold traces with code-computed milestones checked step by step, five branches and three tiers, and expert certification in which experts solved instances by hand, which addresses the risk this paper names of reference answers derived from the evaluator's own code (p.11).
notes: (1) Key naming clash: the web search note calls this paper 'trashchenkov2026powersystemsagent', but that key exists in no catalogue; the only catalogue entry is 'trashchenkov2026psab' (candidates/engineering_arxiv.json). (2) 'Must' rests on the revised text presenting the private seed and deterministic checks as EngTrace's contamination and verification design: this paper used both in engineering before EngTrace's private-seed pool (D-114, September 2026), so leaving it out would invite an overclaim. If the revision makes no such claim, 'should' would be enough. (3) Its caution that 'a reference answer derived from an evaluator cannot certify it' (p.11, p.13) applies to EngTrace's code-derived gold; EngTrace's expert hand-solving in Layer 2 is the answer to it and could be positioned that way. (4) The benchmark is near ceiling for strong agents (p.10, p.13), and it reports no sampling variance (p.13).
